## In 60 seconds

After ablation, late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and edema-sensitive MRI show the treated tissue [@fusco2024].
Whether they show a gap depends on the gap's width against the image's blur: a narrow gap in a blurred line fills
in. Three months after pulmonary vein isolation, the number of scar gaps on MRI tracked how many veins had
reconnected, but their location agreed only fairly with where veins reconnected (kappa 0.37) [@aljefairi2019]; in
a later trial, lesions did not uniformly become scar [@akoum2024]. Right after ablation, edema makes lesions look
larger than the irreversible injury [@tampakis2023]. Real-time MRI-guided ablation avoids ionizing radiation; in
one early series of typical flutter, acute block was confirmed in 32 of 35 patients and technical challenges
occurred in 19 [@hopman2026]. Its limits are compatible equipment, electrograms recorded under strong
interference, catheter visualization and lesion assessment [@tampakis2023].

## From the field

- **Gaps predict how many, not where.** In 51 patients scanned three months after isolation and then studied
  electrically, scar gaps were found in 76% of patients and 39% of veins, and reconnection in 88% of patients and
  50% of veins. The number of gaps correlated with the extent of reconnection, but location agreement was fair
  (kappa 0.37), and gaps were missed in areas of pre-existing fibrosis [@aljefairi2019].
- **Edema is not scar.** Edema seen on T2-weighted imaging after ablation includes reversible injury and is larger
  than the delayed-enhancement region; it subsides over time, and electrical reconnection can follow
  [@tampakis2023].
- **Isolation despite a gap.** Electrical isolation can be observed even where MRI shows a gap in the tissue
  [@tampakis2023], so an image gap and a reconnected vein answer different questions.
- **Real-time MRI in early use.** In a single-center series of 35 typical-flutter ablations at 1.5 T, acute
  bidirectional block was confirmed in 32; challenges, most often with coronary sinus catheter positioning and
  system integration, occurred in 19; typical flutter recurred in 6 of 32 within a year. The authors describe an
  early implementation phase of a first-generation platform [@hopman2026].
- **Fast anatomy for guidance.** In 42 patients, a 3-D whole-heart scan took about 98 s and automatic meshes of the
  right-sided chambers took about 16 s; ablation followed the predefined line in 62% [@jahnke2024].
- **Frames and tracking.** Real-time images for passive catheter visualization have been reported at 4–8 frames
  per second, and active tracking of tip coils at up to 50 [@tampakis2023].

## Derivations

### When blur hides a gap

Take a straight lesion line of width $w$ with a gap of width $g$ along it, and an image blurred by an isotropic
Gaussian of standard deviation $\sigma$. The 2-D Gaussian is separable, so the blurred image is the blurred band
across the line times one minus the blurred gap along it:

$$
I(x, y) = B(y)\,\bigl[1 - G(x)\bigr], \qquad
I_{\text{line}} = \operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{w}{2\sqrt2\,\sigma}\right), \qquad
I_{\text{gap}} = I_{\text{line}}\left[1 - \operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{g}{2\sqrt2\,\sigma}\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-m53-gap}

where $B$ and $G$ are blurred box profiles, the same error functions as a thin wall in m51
([eq-m51-wall](m51-cardiac-ct.qmd#eq-m51-wall)). With a threshold $\theta$ (here half the contrast), the gap is
visible when $I_{\text{gap}} < \theta$, that is when
$g > 2\sqrt2\,\sigma\,\operatorname{erfinv}(1 - \theta/I_{\text{line}})$. LGE resolution is about 1.5–2 mm
routinely and about 1 mm when thin walls are the target [@kellman2012]; for a 4-mm line (illustrative), the
smallest visible gap is 0.57, 0.86 and 1.12 mm at 1, 1.5 and 2 mm blur (lab part A). If acute edema extends a
margin $e$ beyond each lesion, a gap appears as $\max(0, g - 2e)$ (lab part D).

::: {.demo #m53-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m53-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m53-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m53-d1-gap.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m53-gap for a straight band with a rectangular gap and an isotropic Gaussian blur; tested against
  `epml.lesion`.
- The visibility threshold is half the full contrast. The blur range covers the published LGE resolutions
  [@kellman2012]; line and gap widths are illustrative.
- What it ignores: noise, curvature of real lines, partial volume across the wall's thickness, edema, and
  lesions whose signal is not uniform.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A gap narrower than about the blur width fills in.
- A thin or faint line can vanish with its gaps.

### Gaps against reconnection

An image gap is anatomy; reconnection is physiology. Agreement between them per vein or per segment is measured
with Cohen's kappa ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)). In a simulation where gaps 1 mm or wider usually
conduct and veins also reconnect for other reasons, even a perfect image of every gap reached a kappa of only 0.63,
and blurring away gaps too thin to conduct could raise the agreement slightly (lab part C; all probabilities
illustrative). The clinical figure, 0.37 for location [@aljefairi2019], mixes these effects with registration,
pre-existing fibrosis and timing.

**Key takeaways**

- Kappa measures agreement between two different questions, not the scanner alone.
- Thin gaps, recovery and pre-existing fibrosis all separate the image from the electrogram.

### Real-time MRI: frames and tracking

A real-time image is acquired line by line, one repetition time TR apart. With $N_{\text{lines}}$ lines and an
acceleration factor $R$,

$$
T_{\text{frame}} = \frac{N_{\text{lines}}\,\mathrm{TR}}{R}, \qquad \text{frame rate} = \frac{1}{T_{\text{frame}}}, \qquad
d = v\,T_{\text{frame}}
$$ {#eq-m53-frame}

where $d$ is how far a structure moving at speed $v$ travels during one frame. With 64 lines and an illustrative TR
of 3 ms, a frame takes 192 ms, about 5 frames per second, inside the 4–8 reported for passive catheter
visualization; active tracking of a few tip coils has been reported at up to 50 updates per second
[@tampakis2023]. For scale, coronary arteries moved 22–70 mm/s in plane [@achenbach2000], so 9 mm per 192-ms frame
at their average speed.

::: {.demo #m53-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m53-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m53-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m53-d2-frame-rate.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m53-frame for single-shot line-by-line acquisition; tested against `epml.lesion`.
- Reported rates are from a review [@tampakis2023]; speeds are the published coronary averages [@achenbach2000].
  Repetition times, line counts and acceleration factors are illustrative.
- What it ignores: non-Cartesian and partial acquisitions, view sharing, reconstruction latency and the time to
  display and act on an image.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Fewer lines or more acceleration buy frames at the cost of resolution or signal.
- Tracking a point is much faster than imaging a plane.

### Electrograms inside the scanner

Electrograms recorded during scanning carry magnetohydrodynamic voltages from flowing blood, RF pickup and voltages
induced by gradient switching. One setup combined RF filtering with a 300 Hz low-pass, a 30 Hz high-pass and a
60 Hz notch, and obtained the best signals with a 120 Hz low-pass despite lower amplitude [@tampakis2023]. In lab
part F, with illustrative waveforms, the 120 Hz low-pass left about a third of the residual interference of
300 Hz but shrank the electrogram from 1.64 to 1.48 mV peak to peak. Filters that remove interference also remove
signal, which matters most for low-amplitude potentials (m03, m14).

**Key takeaways**

- Scanner interference overlaps the electrogram's band, so filtering always trades signal for noise.
- Interpretation of low-amplitude signals is the first casualty.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where lesion imaging shows up in EP.** Studies image lesions after pulmonary vein isolation and compare gaps with
reconnection at a repeat procedure [@aljefairi2019], examine whether lesions became scar in a trial
[@akoum2024], and describe edema and enhancement after ablation [@fusco2024; @tampakis2023]. Real-time MRI-guided
ablation has been reported in typical atrial flutter [@hopman2026; @jahnke2024; @tampakis2023].

**What the evidence is.** Lesion-gap studies are single-center cohorts with a repeat electrophysiological study as
the reference [@aljefairi2019]. The real-time MRI reports are single-center series and reviews of feasibility,
and in humans the cited reports are all in typical flutter [@hopman2026; @jahnke2024; @tampakis2023]. None is a randomized
comparison with conventional guidance.

**What a reader should ask:**

- **When was the scan?** Acute edema, early enhancement and chronic scar show different things [@tampakis2023].
- **How wide must a gap be to be seen?** Compare it with the resolution (@eq-m53-gap).
- **Agreement with what, at what level?** Per patient, per vein or per segment changes the answer
  [@aljefairi2019].

## How experts think

Before trusting an image of an ablation line, ask:

1. **Is the gap wider than the blur?** If not, the image cannot show it (@eq-m53-gap).
2. **Is this edema or scar?** Acute imaging overstates the lesion [@tampakis2023].
3. **Was pre-existing fibrosis there?** It hides gaps on LGE [@aljefairi2019].
4. **Is the agreement per vein or per segment?** Extent and location can disagree [@aljefairi2019].
5. **For real-time guidance, how fast is the loop?** Frame time and tracking rate set what the operator
   sees (@eq-m53-frame).

One sentence to keep: **an image gap is anatomy seen through blur and edema at one moment; reconnection is
conduction measured later.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Gap in a blurred line (@eq-m53-gap) | line $\operatorname{erf}(w/(2\sqrt2\sigma))$; gap center line $\times\,[1 - \operatorname{erf}(g/(2\sqrt2\sigma))]$; visible if $g > 2\sqrt2\sigma\,\operatorname{erfinv}(1 - \theta/I_{\text{line}})$ |
| Edema margin $e$ | apparent gap $\max(0, g - 2e)$ |
| Real-time frame (@eq-m53-frame) | $T = N\,\mathrm{TR}/R$; motion per frame $vT$ |
| Agreement | Cohen's kappa ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)) |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| LGE resolution 1.5–2 mm routinely, about 1 mm for thin walls | @kellman2012 |
| 4–8 frames/s passive visualization; up to 50/s active tracking | @tampakis2023 |
| Filter chain 300 Hz low-pass, 30 Hz high-pass, 60 Hz notch; best at 120 Hz low-pass | @tampakis2023 |
| Coronary in-plane speed 22.4–69.5 mm/s | @achenbach2000 |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Derive the signal at the center of a gap in a blurred lesion line.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The line minus the gap is a band times one minus a box; a separable Gaussian blur gives
$B(y)[1 - G(x)]$, so at the center it is $\operatorname{erf}(w/(2\sqrt2\sigma))\,[1 -
\operatorname{erf}(g/(2\sqrt2\sigma))]$ (@eq-m53-gap).

</details>

**Q2. Your LGE resolution is 2 mm. Can you see a 0.5-mm gap?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not with a half-contrast threshold: for a 4-mm line the smallest visible gap at 2-mm blur is about
1.1 mm (@eq-m53-gap). A narrower gap reads as a continuous line.

</details>

**Q3. Why might an MRI taken the day after ablation show no gaps, yet a vein reconnects?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Acute edema makes lesions look wider than the irreversible injury, narrowing or closing gaps on the image; as it
resolves, tissue can recover and conduct [@tampakis2023]. A gap narrower than the blur is also invisible.

</details>

**Q4. Image gaps predicted the number of reconnected veins but not their location. How can both be true?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A patient with more lesion damage overall has more of both, so counts correlate; but placing a gap on the right
segment needs resolution, registration and correct handling of pre-existing fibrosis, where gaps were missed
[@aljefairi2019]. Location agreement was fair (kappa 0.37).

</details>

**Q5. Why use kappa rather than percent agreement?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Because two findings that are each common agree often by chance; kappa subtracts the agreement expected by chance
([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)).

</details>

**Q6. A real-time sequence uses 96 lines at a TR of 2.5 ms with no acceleration. What is the frame rate?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$96 \times 2.5$ = 240 ms per frame, about 4.2 frames per second (@eq-m53-frame): at the low end of the reported
4–8 for passive visualization [@tampakis2023].

</details>

**Q7. Why can active tracking update so much faster than imaging?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It locates a few small coils at the catheter tip from short projections instead of acquiring every line of a
plane, so each update needs far less data; rates up to 50 per second have been reported [@tampakis2023].

</details>

**Q8. What disturbs an electrogram inside an MRI scanner, and what does filtering cost?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Magnetohydrodynamic voltages from flowing blood, RF pickup and gradient-induced voltages [@tampakis2023]. Filters
that remove them also remove part of the electrogram; one setup found the best signals at a 120 Hz low-pass despite
lower amplitude. Low-amplitude potentials suffer first.

</details>

**Q9. What would you need before using MRI lesion imaging as a procedural endpoint?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Evidence that the acute image predicts durable lesions and outcome, a resolution that shows the gaps that
matter (@eq-m53-gap), a sequence that separates edema from necrosis and can be repeated, and a prospective comparison with
the current endpoint. The cited work does not yet provide this [@tampakis2023; @aljefairi2019].

</details>

**Q10. What did the early real-time MRI flutter series report, and how should it be read?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Acute block in 32 of 35, challenges in 19, no major complications and recurrence in 6 of 32 within a year
[@hopman2026]. It is a retrospective single-center series of a first-generation platform: evidence of feasibility,
not of superiority.

</details>

**Q11. What did a lesion analysis inside a randomized trial add?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

That ablation lesions did not uniformly become scar on follow-up MRI, with large differences between centers
[@akoum2024]: delivery and measurement both vary.

</details>

**Q12. You blur away thin gaps and agreement with reconnection goes up. Is the scanner better?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

No. Thin gaps that do not conduct were disagreements; hiding them raises kappa without making the image more
accurate (lab part C). Agreement depends on what the reference measures.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab goes from a single gap to a ring of lesions, then to real-time imaging and electrograms in the scanner.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | When blur hides a gap (@eq-m53-gap) | published resolutions |
| B | Gaps in a ring lesion around a vein | our own phantom |
| C | Image gaps against reconnection (kappa, m35) | our own simulation |
| D | Acute edema and apparent gaps | our own model |
| E | Real-time MRI frame budget (@eq-m53-frame) | published frame rates |
| F | Electrograms during scanning | published filter chain, our own signals |
| G | Reading the evidence | published results |

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. At the center of a very wide gap, what is the signal?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Zero: $\operatorname{erf}(g/(2\sqrt2\sigma)) \to 1$ (@eq-m53-gap).

</details>

**S2. A gap of 3 mm with an edema margin of 1 mm on each side looks how wide?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1 mm.

</details>

**S3. 128 lines at TR 3 ms with acceleration 2: frame time?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

192 ms (@eq-m53-frame).

</details>

**S4. A tracked tip updates 50 times a second. How long between updates?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

20 ms.

</details>

**S5. Two raters agree on 90% of veins. Is their kappa 0.9?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Not necessarily: kappa subtracts chance agreement, which is high when one answer is common
([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-kappa)).

</details>

**S6. True or false: a lower low-pass cut-off always gives a better electrogram.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. It removes more interference and more of the signal; the best setting depends on what must be seen
[@tampakis2023].

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Real-time MRI-guided ablation.** Tampakis and colleagues show an interventional MRI suite, electrograms
  disturbed by gradients, and images of flutter lesions before and after ablation, with edema and enhancement
  [@tampakis2023; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10600785/)]. This module: real-time MRI
  and electrograms inside the scanner.
- **Meshes for guidance.** Jahnke and colleagues report the whole-heart scan, the automatic segmentation and meshes
  used for navigation, and how closely ablation followed the planned line [@jahnke2024;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11026457/)]. This module: from the field.

## Further reading

- **Lesions and gaps.** Gaps against reconnection [@aljefairi2019]; lesions in a trial [@akoum2024]; edema and
  enhancement after ablation [@fusco2024; @tampakis2023].
- **Real-time MRI.** Review [@tampakis2023]; early clinical series [@hopman2026]; meshes for guidance
  [@jahnke2024]; resolution of LGE [@kellman2012].
- **Related modules.** m27 and m28 for how lesions form, m51 for the thin-wall blur model, m52 for LGE physics,
  m35 for kappa, m03 and m14 for electrogram filtering, and m49 for the fluoroscopy that MRI guidance avoids.
